title: Jane Goodall: All Good
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck profile primatologist Jane Goodall: her unconventional start under Louis Leakey in Gombe, Tanzania, her close habituation of chimpanzees (naming them, feeding bananas), the discovery of tool use and chimpanzee culture, her family life and marriages, the F family and Frodo, the Gombe chimpanzee war, her later regrets about methods, and her advocacy and communication work. The episode also includes a Far Side cease-and-desist anecdote and a listener mail about grit versus conscientiousness.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, joke about being tired, and mention the 2017 documentary about Jane Goodall.

segments.title: Introduction to Jane Goodall
segments.summary: Chuck introduces Jane Goodall as a primatologist who learned in the field without formal training; Louis Leakey hired her on purpose because he wanted an untrained observer. Josh gives her birth in 1934 in England, her parents, and her mother's encouragement.

segments.title: Childhood love of animals
segments.summary: The hosts describe Goodall's childhood fascination with animals, including her hen-house observation and patient pig-watching, and contrast her approach with the detached methods biologists were trained to use.

segments.title: Detachment versus anthropomorphism
segments.summary: Chuck explains the scientific fear of anthropomorphizing animals and why researchers avoided attachment, which Goodall departed from. Josh describes her early memories of worms and her five hours in a hen house.

segments.title: Arrival in Africa with Leakey
segments.summary: Leakey hires Goodall, who had been his secretary, and she goes to Tanzania at age 26 in 1960 with her mother as required chaperone. They have a cook, Dominic, and both catch malaria; Dominic nurses them.

segments.title: Gombe fieldwork and winning trust
segments.summary: Goodall's mother helps set up a medical camp and leaves after about four months. Goodall waits months to see chimps, then wins their trust by going barefoot and acting like a peer in the trees. Josh notes her confidence despite snakes and other dangers.

segments.title: David Greybeard and feeding bananas
segments.summary: After five months, the chimp David Greybeard approaches her and takes bananas, and the others follow. Goodall had given names to the chimps, which academics criticized, along with feeding them.

segments.title: Chimpanzee social structure
segments.summary: Goodall names chimps and tracks family lines by letter (the F family). She discovers complex social hierarchies, alliances, and territories.

segments.title: Tool use and chimpanzee culture
segments.summary: Goodall observes chimps modifying grass and sticks to fish termites, showing tool use. Leakey declared that humans must redefine tool or accept chimps as human. Different groups use tools differently, which the hosts describe as culture.

segments.title: National Geographic filmmaker and marriage
segments.summary: In 1962 National Geographic sent Dutch filmmaker Hugo van Lawick. Goodall was reluctant but accepted the funding; they fell in love and had a son, nicknamed Grub. Goodall says raising her son helped her understand chimp mothers. The 1963 National Geographic cover story made her known.

segments.title: Media attention and the Far Side cartoon
segments.summary: Press coverage framed Goodall in terms of her looks, which bothered her but drew attention to her cause. Gary Larson's Far Side cartoon about a chimp and a blonde hair prompted a cease-and-desist letter from the Jane Goodall Institute, later resolved warmly. Chuck notes she is in her nineties.

segments.title: Education, books, and marriage breakdown
segments.summary: Goodall publishes In the Shadow of Man in 1971 and gets a PhD from Cambridge. She worked at Stanford and the University of Dar es Salaam while staying based at Gombe. Her marriage with van Lawick ended amid work and life strains.

segments.title: Gombe Research Center and Derek Bryceson
segments.summary: Goodall founds the Gombe Stream Research Center; she marries Derek Bryceson, who helps turn the reserve into a national park. He dies of cancer five years later. The hosts discuss her decades of research and the Trimates.

segments.title: The Trimates
segments.summary: Leakey hired Diane Fossey (gorillas) and Biruté Galdikas (orangutans). Together with Goodall they were called the Trimates.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts transition with a short break and mention a brief pivot to serious discussion.

segments.title: The F family and Flo
segments.summary: Flo, mother of several chimps, was central to Goodall's understanding of family structure. Her children included Fifi, who became dominant female and had nine offspring, and Freud, who became dominant male in 1993.

segments.title: Frodo and the question of killing him
segments.summary: Frodo, son of Fifi, was a violent chimp who bullied Goodall and killed a 14-month-old toddler in 2002. Goodall defended him, and some argued he should be put down; the hosts weigh both sides.

segments.title: Gombe chimpanzee war and later reflections
segments.summary: After the Kasakela group split in 1971, a war broke out, starting with the 1974 killing of Godi. Goodall later said she would do some things differently. The hosts note she remains active through the Jane Goodall Institute and her podcast, which ended in 2022.

segments.title: Wrap-up of Goodall discussion
segments.summary: Chuck concludes that Goodall is loved worldwide despite academic criticism and points listeners to her books and podcast.

segments.title: Listener mail: grit versus conscientiousness
segments.summary: A listener writes about grit as distinct from conscientiousness, describing working while putting himself through engineering college. The hosts respond and invite emails.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits and promotion for iHeartRadio.
